newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: PM CALLS FOR WIDE DEBATE ON TAX REFORM
The Prime Minister has told a group of small business leaders that Australia needs to be willing to examine, and change if necessary, some of Australia's economic structures.
John Howard told the Sydney meeting the tax system needs an overhaul, and he called for wide and comprehensive public debate on the issue.
Mr Howard says changes to the system shouldn't be made out of some blind commitment to ideology.
He says they should promote a job-generating system which will increase the competitiveness of the economy, and increase living standards.
The Prime Minister says he remains committed to honouring his promise not to introduce a GST in his first term.
MINISTER REJECTS COWLEY'S CONCERN OVER PACKER DEAL
The federal Communications Minister, Senator Richard Alston, has rejected New Limited chief Ken Cowley's concerns that a deal has been done with Kerry Packer over media ownership.

Senator Alston says the Government heralded a review of the cross-media ownership laws before coming to power and he doesn't think there has been anything unusual about the process that's been followed.
Senator Alston, Jamie Packer and Australia's key media executives gathered for a lunch today in support of the Hollows Foundation but Senator Alston says the cross-media rules were not discussed.
GOVT UNVEILS FIRST PART OF NEWCASTLE ASSISTANCE PACKAGE
Employment Minister Amanda Vanstone has unveiled more than two million dollars in funding for job creation in the Hunter region, as the first part of the Government's response to the BHP closure.
The money will go towards training and business programs.
Senator Vanstone visited Newcastle today, discussing the Government's 10 million dollar assistance package.
More than half the money will go to a labour market program known as the New Enterprise incentive scheme to enable 100 new small businesses to set up in the region.
Meanwhile, workers at BHP's Whyalla steelworks in South Australia have walked off the job for 24 hours following a mass meeting this morning.
IMMIGRATION CUTS NOT DUE TO HANSON'S COMMENTS: RUDDOCK
The Immigration Minister has denied that new plans to cut Australia's immigration intake aren't a response to Pauline Hanson's views.
Under the plan, Australia will accept six-thousand fewer immigrants in 1997-1998, with the program set at 68-thousand for the next year.
Phillip Ruddock says the reductions are being made because of concern over the high level of unemployment.
Mr Ruddock says another contributor is the fact that the employment experience of immigrants through the unskilled stream has been very unsatisfactory.
Under the new plan more than 50 per cent of migrants will have to be skilled.
PLEA FOR KIDNAPPERS TO CONTACT POLICE
The New South Wales Premier is appealing for witnesses of a kidnapping in Parramatta earlier this month to come forward.
Police hold grave fears for the 39-year-old victims safety. Detectives say Kerry Whelan of Kurrajong, north-west of Sydney, was abducted from a Parramatta car park on May the sixth.
The kidnappers asked her husband Bernard Whelan, senior executive of a machinery company, for a large sum of money.
Mr Whelan was ready to meet some of the demands, but the ransom deadline passed without the kidnappers making further contact.
Police have appealed to the abductors to make contact again.
CRA ANNUAL MEETING ENDS AFTER NOISY PROTESTS
Mining company CRA's annual shareholders meeting has ended, after several hours of noisy and often bitter exchanges between the chairman and protestors.

Unions alleged discrimination against their members while conservationists attacked alleged environmental degradation and human rights abuses by the Indonesian military at the Freeport Copper Mine in Irian Jaya.
Chairman, John Uhrig, was involved in several heated clashes although he said afterwards the protestors showed "improved behaviour" compared to last year.
